toc.title: Safety first, then a light touch

blocks.p: Our bodies are naturally compelled to self-regulate and release trauma. It's called homeostasis. But you might be worried about touching upon your stuck defensive state, or allowing yourself to feel it. Here's how it might actually be helpful to touch upon it lightly, and how you could approach that.
A member of my community pointed out that as humans, we have a little more agency: we can do conscious work to get to a safe and social state.

We can. Our bodies are compelled to self-regulate. I think our thoughts kind of get in the way, in a sense. So do our behavioral adaptations, and so do our cognitive adaptations. But the natural inclination is to self-regulate. We must do so. Then trauma gets in the way.

To unlock that natural self-regulation capacity and compulsion, I think about it as aligning our thoughts with our body. That's why I think mindfulness can help so much. It quiets the thoughts down enough to be in tune with what's happening bottom up. Now you're connecting your cognitions with your experience, your felt experience. And if the cognitions aren't getting in the way anymore, or the behavioral adaptations, then self-regulation naturally unfolds after that, and you're more of a witness to it than a director of it.

Quieting the cognitions, or aligning them with what's happening bottom up, helps you step closer to the body's natural self-regulation. I call it a compulsion: we have to, in order to survive, and at least to live optimally.
Another member summed it up: so trust it.

Yes. I wrote and recorded a guided practice for mindfully experiencing the stuck defensive state. Don't do something like that until you're there. It builds on everything that comes before it, so make sure you're anchored in safety first.

The practice was about pendulating: can we feel our defensive state and our safety state, and can we move from safety to defense and back? It was also about mindfully experiencing and building the felt sense of what's happening inside.

It ends like this. There might be an impulse that arises from your mindful experiencing, and if you feel that impulse, let it happen. You might see that the defensive state and the safety state start to interact. There may be a shift that happens, and if there is, you just sit back, trust, and watch. You allow it to unfold, you allow an impulse to emerge, and then you act on it.

Trust is a big part of that. That's why it's so important that the safety state is developed enough to handle it, so you can know: "Oh, I'm watching my self-regulation unfold. I'm just an observer who's experiencing it. I need to step back as much as I can consciously and allow this process to happen, and be a mindful observer of my body's natural self-regulation process."

The first time I did that, fear came up. I was doing a meditation, mindful felt sense kind of stuff, and fear came up in me. If I hadn't been able to tolerate the fear, the immobilization, flight, fight, I easily would've just opened my eyes and walked away and never come back to it.

If the safety state's developed enough, then you might be able to notice whatever stuck defensive state you have when it comes up, and stick with it. You can feel it, mindfully experience it, and allow the internal self-regulation to happen. The safety state is so important in being able to do that.

That's why I implore everybody: make sure you have the polyvagal information, make sure you can anchor in safety, and then lightly step into your stuck defensive state as you're ready to. A lot of it is trusting and witnessing.
Another member added: and respecting. Absolutely.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: Safety first, then a light touch

blocks.p: All of these are safety state things. They come after the safety state's developed enough. Then you can say, "Oh, now I'm a witness. I have trust. I have curiosity." If you have those things and can maintain them, that's a clue that maybe you're ready for something more, and it might be time to start delving into the defensive state.
I think there can be a utility to working on your safety state and then testing it out:

ol: Build safety. Anchor in safety, and practice, practice, practice.
Check where you're at. Ask, "Am I able to feel some of my defensive stuff and maintain it?" Maybe, "Where am I at when it comes to this numbness? What does that feel like?"
Have an exit. Have a plan of action for how you're going to touch into it, and then go do something that's more anchoring.
Touch upon it lightly, then come back to safety. Just start feeling it out, instead of going all the way into it.

blocks.p: I do this in therapy, where we work on safety and then just touch upon defense lightly and see what the capacity to self-regulate is. It's sort of a self-assessment, a check-in with your distress tolerance. I don't think there's anything wrong with that.

One member asked whether this would strengthen the vagal brake. Exactly. As long as you're doing it with curiosity, and then re-grounding in safety, it absolutely could help build the vagal brake, or help build distress tolerance.

If you're touching upon it and you get spiraled into actual dysregulation, that would not be building. Depending on how intense it is, that could potentially be re-traumatizing. If your safety work is successful, then you should be able to lightly touch upon your defensive state with curiosity, without getting spun into dysregulation.
A member added that it's also a matter of knowing when to take a pause:

q: I tend to push through things, and in this work, I need to learn how not to push through, because it can be re-traumatizing. It can be dysregulating for me, and then it takes me a couple of days to recover from that. And as far as the safety part is concerned, for me it's about feeling safe enough. I can get into it feeling safe enough, and then when it's starting to push back, that's kind of how it senses for me. When it's starting to push back, it's time to stop.

blocks.p: Knowing when to stop and when to start matters, whether it's a meditation, a guided practice, or more actively, consciously self-regulating. By then, the basics should already be in place, like your passive safety environment.

If you're curious about your defensive state and want to lightly touch upon it, I don't think it's a bad idea in general. But you have to be really sure that you're able to handle that, lightly, with curiosity, and have an exit plan for it. That I'll leave up to you.
That member noticed I kept saying "with curiosity," and asked: as opposed to what?

As opposed to feeling like you have to. It could be opposed to a lot of things. It might be, "This other member of my group is making more progress than me. I should be doing the same thing." That's more of a pressure, an "I have to," or a competitive kind of thing. Versus, "I just want to know what the heck I feel like. I'm genuinely curious."
So there are a lot of alternatives: competition, pressure, self-judgment, stuff like that. I have to trust that each person knows what curiosity feels like for them.

Irene Lyon put the curious approach playfully when she was on the podcast: "Can you party with that sensation? Have a little party with it." ([Episode 38](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/03e4545e-9525-42ef-9551-e5b3362169b6))
